pairs.question: What can I expect when I quit smoking?
pairs.answer: Quitting smoking is one of the best things you will ever do for your health. Withdrawal can be challenging, but it can help if you look at the symptoms as signs that your body is recovering.
pairs.evidence: Quitting smoking is one of the best things you will ever do for your health. Withdrawal can be challenging, but it can help if you look at the symptoms as signs that your body is recovering.

pairs.question: What are some common withdrawal symptoms?
pairs.answer: Common symptoms include cravings, restlessness, trouble concentrating or sleeping, irritability, anxiety, increases in appetite and weight gain. It's normal to experience these as your body adjusts.
pairs.evidence: Common symptoms include: cravings, restlessness, trouble concentrating or sleeping, irritability, anxiety, increases in appetite and weight gain.

pairs.question: How long do withdrawal symptoms last?
pairs.answer: Many people find withdrawal symptoms disappear completely after two to four weeks. However, for some people, they may last longer.
pairs.evidence: Many people find withdrawal symptoms disappear completely after two to four weeks, although for some people they may last longer.

pairs.question: Is there support available to help me quit?
pairs.answer: Yes, Quitline is available to help you quit from 8am to 8pm, Monday to Friday. It's a great resource to have during your quitting journey.
pairs.evidence: Quitline is available to help you quit, 8am – 8pm, Monday to Friday.

pairs.question: How can I manage cravings?
pairs.answer: Changing your routine can help avoid those triggers that tell your brain it’s time for a smoke. It’s a good strategy to consider as you quit.
pairs.evidence: Changing your routine can help avoid those triggers that tell your brain it’s time for a smoke.

pairs.question: What should I know about weight gain when quitting?
pairs.answer: Many people experience increases in appetite and weight gain when they quit smoking. It's a common part of the process, so be prepared for it.
pairs.evidence: Common symptoms include: cravings, restlessness, trouble concentrating or sleeping, irritability, anxiety, increases in appetite and weight gain.

pairs.question: I've been feeling really restless and having trouble sleeping since I quit. Is that normal?
pairs.answer: Yes, restlessness and trouble concentrating or sleeping are common symptoms when you quit smoking. They will pass as your body gets used to not smoking, and relaxation and deep breathing can help.
pairs.evidence: restlessness and trouble concentrating or sleeping – these will pass as your body gets used to not smoking.

pairs.question: I'm worried about gaining weight after quitting. Is that common?
pairs.answer: Yes, an increase in appetite and weight gain may last several weeks after quitting. Planning ahead can help manage this.
pairs.evidence: increase in appetite and weight gain – this may last several weeks. Planning ahead can help.

pairs.question: How long will these withdrawal symptoms last?
pairs.answer: Symptoms may last longer, but as time passes, you will find they grow weaker, and you will think about smoking less.
pairs.evidence: As time passes, you will find these symptoms grow weaker, and you will think about smoking less.

pairs.question: I've heard caffeine can affect me differently now that I quit smoking. Is that true?
pairs.answer: Yes, caffeine and alcohol are affected by tobacco smoke. It's recommended to cut down on drinks or foods with caffeine when you stop smoking.
pairs.evidence: Caffeine (for example, in coffee, chocolate and cola soft drinks) and alcohol are also affected by tobacco smoke. Cutting down on drinks or foods with caffeine when you stop smoking is recommended.

pairs.question: What should I do if my symptoms are really severe?
pairs.answer: If you have severe or long-lasting symptoms, it might help to discuss them with a health professional or a counsellor.
pairs.evidence: If you have severe or long-lasting symptoms, it might help to discuss them with a health professional or a counsellor.

pairs.question: What should I know about my emotions when I quit smoking?
pairs.answer: In the first days and weeks when you quit smoking, the emotional ups and downs could feel like a rollercoaster ride. It's normal to feel this way as you make big changes in your life.
pairs.evidence: In the first days and weeks when you quit smoking, the emotional ups and downs could feel like a rollercoaster ride.

pairs.question: Will I feel like I'm losing something when I quit smoking?
pairs.answer: Some people describe giving up smoking as feeling like you’re losing a friend. Understanding that this is just a stage can help you through the hard times.
pairs.evidence: Some people describe giving up smoking as feeling like you’re losing a friend.

pairs.question: How quickly will my body start to recover after quitting?
pairs.answer: Your heart rate will slow and your blood pressure will become more stable shortly after quitting. This is a positive sign of recovery.
pairs.evidence: your heart rate will slow and your blood pressure will become more stable.

pairs.question: What happens to the nicotine in my body when I quit?
pairs.answer: Your bloodstream will be almost nicotine free, and the level of carbon monoxide in your blood will have dropped. This helps oxygen reach your heart and muscles more easily.
pairs.evidence: your bloodstream will be almost nicotine free, the level of carbon monoxide in your blood will have dropped, and oxygen will be reaching your heart and muscles more easily.

pairs.question: Will my sense of taste and smell improve after quitting?
pairs.answer: Yes, your sense of taste and smell may have improved after you quit smoking. This is a nice benefit of stopping.
pairs.evidence: your sense of taste and smell may have improved.

pairs.question: What physical improvements can I expect after quitting?
pairs.answer: You will be coughing and wheezing less, and your immune function and circulation to your hands and feet will be improving. Your lungs will also get better at removing mucus, tar, and dust.
pairs.evidence: you will be coughing and wheezing less, your immune function and circulation to your hands and feet will be improving, and your lungs will be getting better at removing mucus, tar and dust.

pairs.question: How will quitting affect my stress levels?
pairs.answer: Your stress levels are likely to have dropped after quitting smoking. You may also notice you're less likely to be coughing up phlegm.
pairs.evidence: your stress levels are likely to have dropped, and you are less likely to be coughing up phlegm.

pairs.question: What long-term health benefits can I expect from quitting smoking?
pairs.answer: Your risk of heart disease will have dropped significantly after quitting, and it will continue to do so over time. This is a major health benefit.
pairs.evidence: your risk of heart disease will have dropped significantly (and will continue to do so over time).

pairs.question: What happens to my risk of heart disease if I quit smoking?
pairs.answer: Your risk of heart disease will have dropped significantly and will continue to do so over time. That's a positive change for your heart health!
pairs.evidence: your risk of heart disease will have dropped significantly (and will continue to do so over time).

pairs.question: If I quit smoking, will my risk of cervical cancer change?
pairs.answer: Yes, a woman’s risk of cervical cancer will be the same as if she had never smoked. That's an important benefit of quitting!
pairs.evidence: a woman’s risk of cervical cancer will be the same as if she had never smoked.

pairs.question: How does quitting smoking affect my risk of lung cancer?
pairs.answer: Your risk of lung cancer will be half that of someone of a similar age who keeps smoking. That's a significant reduction!
pairs.evidence: your risk of lung cancer will be half that of someone of a similar age who keeps smoking.

pairs.question: What about my risk of heart attack and stroke after quitting?
pairs.answer: Your risk of heart attack and stroke will be similar to that of someone who has never smoked. That's a great reason to quit!
pairs.evidence: your risk of heart attack and stroke will be similar to that of someone who has never smoked.

pairs.question: Is weight gain common when I quit smoking?
pairs.answer: Weight gain is not always part of quitting smoking, but it is common. You might feel hungrier than usual after you quit.
pairs.evidence: Weight gain is not always part of quitting smoking but it is common.

pairs.question: What should I do if I feel overwhelmed after quitting?
pairs.answer: In the early days, try not to be too hard on yourself. By quitting smoking, you’re doing great things for your health!
pairs.evidence: in the early days, try not to be too hard on yourself. By quitting smoking you’re doing great things for your health.

pairs.question: I keep getting cravings. How long do they usually last?
pairs.answer: If you can delay acting on a craving for five minutes, it will usually pass. It's tough, but you can do it!
pairs.evidence: delay acting on the craving for five minutes and it will usually pass

pairs.question: What can I do in the morning instead of smoking?
pairs.answer: First thing in the morning, try having a shower instead of reaching for a cigarette. It can help you start your day fresh!

pairs.question: I always want to smoke with my coffee. Any tips?
pairs.answer: Change to a different drink, a different cup, or change where you drink it. This can help break the routine that triggers cravings.
pairs.evidence: with coffee or tea – change to a different drink, a different cup, or change where you drink it

pairs.question: What should I do during my morning tea break?
pairs.answer: During morning tea, try sitting in a different place or with different people, or read a magazine. It can help distract you from cravings.

pairs.question: I work from home and feel the urge to smoke. What can I do?
pairs.answer: At the computer at home, consider moving your desk or redecorating to change the look. A new environment can help reduce cravings.
pairs.evidence: at the computer at home – move your desk or redecorate to change the look

pairs.question: What can I do after work instead of smoking?
pairs.answer: After work, try exercising or meditating. These activities can help you unwind and keep your mind off smoking.

pairs.question: I usually smoke before dinner. What can I do instead?
pairs.answer: Make your dinner time earlier. This simple change can help you avoid the urge to smoke.

pairs.question: What should I do when I'm watching TV and feel like smoking?
pairs.answer: When you're in front of the television, try moving the furniture around, holding a stress ball, or doing some easy stretches. It can help keep your hands busy!

pairs.question: I've been feeling really stressed since I quit smoking. Is that normal?
pairs.answer: Yes, it's common to feel more stressed when you quit smoking. People who smoke tend to have higher stress levels than non-smokers. Most people find that their stress levels are lower six months after quitting than they were before they quit.
pairs.evidence: Most people find that their stress levels are lower six months after quitting than they were before they quit.

pairs.question: I keep having cravings. How can I distract myself?
pairs.answer: It's great to have options! You can ask a friend for a shoulder massage, do a jigsaw puzzle, or think about the reasons you're quitting. Each time you resist the urge, it's a victory.
pairs.evidence: The more options you have to distract yourself, the better.

pairs.question: Is it okay to feel like I need a cigarette when I'm stressed?
pairs.answer: Yes, many people feel that way because the stress-release from smoking is only temporary. It doesn't solve your problems; it just shifts your focus.
pairs.evidence: The stress-release you feel when you have a cigarette is only temporary.

pairs.question: How long will it take for my stress levels to go down after quitting?
pairs.answer: Most people find that their stress levels are lower six months after quitting than they were before they quit. It takes time to settle into new routines.

pairs.question: How can I help myself relax after quitting smoking?
pairs.answer: Consider having a warm drink or reading a book before bed. These activities can help you unwind and manage stress.

pairs.question: How much money can I save if I quit smoking?
pairs.answer: If you smoke a pack of 20 cigarettes a day at $27, you will save around $10,000 a year. That's a lot of money you could use for other things!
pairs.evidence: If you smoke a pack of 20 cigarettes a day at $27, you will save around $10,000 a year.

pairs.question: Will exercising get easier if I quit smoking?
pairs.answer: Yes, exercising to increase your fitness will become easier after you quit smoking. It's a great way to improve your health!
pairs.evidence: Exercising to increase your fitness will become easier.

pairs.evidence: Thinking about what else you would like to do with that money can be a great motivator to stick to your quit plan.

pairs.question: What are some hassles I will be free from if I quit smoking?

pairs.question: I’ve tried quitting multiple times but failed. Should I give up?
pairs.answer: Don’t lose hope! It’s common for people to try to quit a number of times before they stop smoking for good. Each attempt is a step closer to success.
pairs.evidence: It’s common for people to try to quit a number of times before they stop smoking for good.

pairs.question: How can I prepare for my next quit attempt?
pairs.answer: Next time you quit, spend some time thinking about what has worked for you in the past. Make plans for what you will do when temptations come up again.
pairs.evidence: Next time you quit, spend some time thinking about what has worked for you in the past, and what challenges caused you to go back to smoking.

pairs.question: What should I do if I feel guilty after smoking?
pairs.answer: Try not to waste your energy on self-blame. Instead, treat that cigarette as a sign to revise your quitting strategy. You can always get back on track!
